cues.text: Imagine you're ordering a replacement phone charger.
You've found the one you need, checked the price, and you're ready to pay.
Above it, a message says you could get free shipping if you spent a little more.
So you go back to browsing and find a cable organizer, add it to the cart, and the delivery charge disappears.
The whole order now costs more than it did with paid shipping.
but you also get another product which can make the extra spending feel easier to justify.
That's how free shipping can change a purchase.
A condition attached to the offer gives you a reason to buy more after you've already found what you needed.
It won't affect every order and qualifying can be a good deal.
The important question is what you buy to get there.
There's an obvious appeal to getting something free.
But researchers have found that zero can behave differently from an ordinary low price.
In a study published in 2007, researchers offered people a choice between a cheaper chocolate and a more expensive one.
